slides.title: Unit Of Compute
slides.lead:
A hypervisor is software that creates and runs multiple virtual machines on one physical server by sharing its resources
An instance is one such virtual machine: a virtual server in the cloud that you rent and pay for as you use it

points.text: Bundles virtual CPU (vCPU), memory, network and storage together
Each instance gets a unique instance ID at launch
Moves through lifecycle states: pending, running, stopped, terminated
One instance is one isolated compute boundary per workload

slides.notes: Explain that an instance bundles compute, memory and storage into one billable unit. Point out the lifecycle states as a common exam question. Mention EC2 as the AWS name for this unit.

slides.label: Analogy: drawing electricity from a utility grid
slides.title: Unit Of Compute
slides.notes: TR analogy: Similar to drawing electricity from a utility grid, compute capacity is used on demand and billed only for the time it is consumed — just as an instance incurs compute charges only while it is running.

slides.title: Request To Running
slides.lead: Provisioning is the automated path from a request to a running instance: a console click or a programmatic call triggers allocation, not weeks of physical setup
slides.notes: Walk through the four steps from request to a reachable instance. Name the EC2 console and the RunInstances API as where this happens in AWS. Ask what happens between clicking launch and the instance becoming reachable.

slides.title: Request To Running

points.text: Request names the image, instance type and network settings
Scheduler picks a physical host with free capacity
Hypervisor boots the virtual machine from the chosen image
Instance enters the running state, then status checks confirm it is healthy
In AWS, this is triggered from the EC2 console or the `RunInstances` Application Programming Interface (API) call

slides.notes: Walk through the four steps from request to a reachable instance. Name the EC2 console and the RunInstances API as where this happens in AWS. Ask what happens between clicking launch and the instance becoming reachable.

slides.title: Where Billing Begins
slides.lead: This on-demand provisioning is what makes elasticity possible: capacity is requested and released in minutes, turning compute into a metered utility rather than a fixed purchase

points.text: Billing starts the moment the instance enters Running state
Terminating an instance returns its capacity to the shared pool
Stopped instances stop compute charges but keep storage billed
No separate fee is charged for provisioning

slides.notes: Stress that billing starts only at Running, not Pending. Point to the lifecycle bar on the diagram. Ask what happens to cost if an instance is left Stopped rather than Terminated.

slides.title: Picking An Instance
slides.lead: A low-traffic web app and a CPU-heavy batch job need different instances, since provisioning lets each request exactly the capacity its load demands
slides.notes: Walk through why the batch job needs sustained compute while the web app only needs light, bursty capacity. Point to the table's vCPU and memory columns. Ask which instance type fits a steady, heavy workload.

slides.title: Picking An Instance
slides.lead: t3 instances are burstable and run on CPU credits, while c5 instances deliver full CPU performance continuously
slides.notes: Walk through why the batch job needs sustained compute while the web app only needs light, bursty capacity. Point to the table's vCPU and memory columns. Ask which instance type fits a steady, heavy workload.

slides.title: Five Resource-Based Types
slides.lead: EC2 instance types are grouped into families, each tuned for a different resource balance (compute, memory, storage, or specialised hardware) based on what its workloads need most

items.title: General Purpose
items.text: Balanced vCPU-to-memory ratio for mixed workloads

items.title: Compute Optimized
items.text: High vCPU-to-memory ratio for CPU-bound tasks

items.title: Memory Optimized
items.text: Large RAM-to-vCPU ratio for in-memory workloads

items.title: Storage Optimized
items.text: Fast local disks for I/O-heavy tasks

items.title: GPU & Accelerator
items.text: Dedicated chips for AI/ML training and inference

slides.notes: Present this as the map of families before going into any one of them in detail. Mention that AWS, Azure and GCP all group instance types this same way, just with different naming letters.

slides.title: Five Resource-Based Types
slides.notes: Present this as the map of families before going into any one of them in detail. Mention that AWS, Azure and GCP all group instance types this same way, just with different naming letters.

slides.title: Balanced Resource Mix
slides.lead: General purpose instances, AWS’s M and T families, offer a balanced ratio of about 4 GB memory per virtual CPU (vCPU), so no single resource is starved for typical mixed workloads

points.text: Typical use: web servers, small-to-medium databases, dev environments
Moderately priced: a sensible default when the main bottleneck is not yet known

slides.notes: Explain that balanced does not mean weak; it means no bottleneck is designed in advance. Ask: why would a web server rarely need the heaviest memory or CPU ratio?

slides.label: Analogy: a family sedan car
slides.title: Balanced Resource Mix
slides.notes: TR analogy: A general-purpose instance is like a family sedan car — not the fastest, not the biggest boot, but balanced for most everyday trips — just as it balances CPU and memory instead of maximising either.

slides.title: High CPU Ratio
slides.lead: Compute optimized instances shift the balance toward more vCPU per gigabyte of memory, suiting workloads limited mainly by processing speed rather than memory

points.text: Typical use: batch processing, video encoding, gaming servers, scientific simulation
Resource ratio: about 2 GB memory per vCPU, half of general purpose
AWS example: the C-family instance types
Cost: lower price per vCPU than general purpose

slides.notes: Contrast directly with the general purpose ratio shown earlier on the same scale image. Point out video encoding and simulation as the canonical interview example of a CPU-bound job.

slides.title: RAM And Disk Focus
slides.lead: Memory optimized instances favour RAM-heavy workloads, while storage optimized instances favour fast local-disk access: two separate bottlenecks that general purpose and compute families do not target
slides.notes: Clarify that storage optimized local disks are ephemeral, unlike the persistent EBS block volumes used for durable data. Point to this table when contrasting memory-heavy and disk-heavy workloads. Exam angle: ask which family suits a Cassandra-style database needing heavy disk I/O.

slides.title: Built For AI/ML
slides.lead: GPU and accelerator instances attach a graphics processing unit (GPU) or a purpose-built AI chip beside the CPU, giving the massively parallel compute that AI/ML workloads need

points.text: Use case: deep learning training, large-scale inference, rendering
AWS examples: P-family (GPU training), G-family (GPU inference/graphics)
Trn-family (Trainium chip for training), Inf-family (Inferentia chip for inference)
Cost: priced well above CPU-only families per running hour

slides.notes: Stress that a GPU instance is still an EC2 instance, just with specialised hardware attached. The memory constraint this hardware introduces is covered separately under sizing.

slides.label: Analogy: a toll plaza of open booths
slides.title: Built For AI/ML
slides.notes: Analogy: A GPU is like a toll plaza with hundreds of open booths letting cars through at the same time, instead of a single booth clearing vehicles one by one — just as thousands of GPU cores process data in parallel, instead of a few CPU cores working through tasks largely in sequence.

slides.title: Four Key Axes
slides.lead: Choosing an instance size means balancing four characteristics together, not picking one number

items.title: vCPU
items.text: Virtual CPU threads allocated to the instance (usually 2 vCPU = 1 physical core)

items.title: Memory
items.text: RAM available for applications and caches

items.title: Network
items.text: Bandwidth for data transfer, measured in Gbps

items.title: Storage
items.text: IOPS and throughput to attached EBS volumes

slides.notes: Introduce the four axes learners will size against before taking each one in turn. Interview angle: naming all four dimensions when asked how to size an instance.

slides.title: Compute And RAM
slides.lead: A virtual CPU (vCPU) is a thread of a physical processor core assigned to one instance; memory is the RAM it can address directly

points.text: vCPU count sets how many parallel threads the instance runs
Memory size limits data held in RAM before swapping or failure
`m6i.xlarge` offers 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB memory
Burstable instances (T-family) earn CPU credits to run above a baseline CPU level

slides.notes: Explain vCPU as a thread, not a full physical core, and memory as the shared workspace it works in. Point to the m6i.xlarge figures as a concrete reference. Exam hook: vCPU versus physical core distinction.

slides.label: Analogy: a student at a study table
slides.title: Compute And RAM
slides.notes: Analogy: A vCPU is like a student working at a study table and memory is the size of that table — just as a bigger table lets students keep more books open without running back to the shelf, more memory lets the vCPUs keep more data ready without slowing down to fetch it from disk.

slides.title: Bandwidth And IOPS
slides.lead: Network and storage characteristics decide how fast data moves to the instance and its attached disks, as a separate limit from vCPU or memory

points.text: Network bandwidth: measured in Gbps, scales with instance size
Baseline bandwidth can burst higher for short periods
EBS-optimized throughput: dedicated MB/s bandwidth to attached volumes
IOPS: input/output operations per second a volume sustains

slides.notes: Clarify that EBS-optimized bandwidth is separate from general network bandwidth, so a storage-heavy job can bottleneck with spare vCPU still free. Exam hook: difference between network Gbps and EBS throughput MB/s.

slides.title: Matching Size To Load
slides.lead: Right-sizing means picking the smallest instance that meets sustained CPU, memory, network and storage needs, checked against real usage data

points.text: AWS Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch metrics for sizing recommendations
Over-provisioning pays for idle capacity every billing hour
Under-provisioning causes throttling, swapping or dropped network packets
Resize by stopping, changing instance type, then restarting

slides.notes: Stress that right-sizing is a recurring check as workload patterns shift, not a one-time launch decision. Reserved pricing only pays off once utilization stays consistently high. Exam hook: name the AWS tool used for sizing recommendations.

slides.title: GPU Memory Limit
slides.lead: Video RAM (VRAM) is the dedicated memory on a GPU that holds model weights and data during AI training or inference, separate from the instance’s system RAM

points.text: VRAM capacity caps the model size a GPU can load
Exceeding VRAM causes an out-of-memory failure, not slowdown
`g5.xlarge`: one NVIDIA A10G GPU with 24 GB VRAM
`g4dn.xlarge`: one NVIDIA T4 GPU with 16 GB VRAM

slides.notes: Emphasise VRAM as a hard ceiling, not a performance dial like vCPU or memory. Point to the two GPU figures as sizing references. Exam hook: why VRAM overflow fails outright instead of degrading gracefully.

slides.label: Analogy: a suitcase of fixed size
slides.title: GPU Memory Limit
slides.notes: Analogy: A suitcase with a fixed size cannot fit more clothes than its capacity, however fast you pack — just as a model larger than the VRAM cannot load, regardless of how fast the GPU is.

slides.title: Two Workload Types
slides.lead: Two workloads illustrate the same sizing method: a web application bound by vCPU and memory, and an inference job bound by VRAM
slides.notes: Walk through both rows: the web app fits comfortably on m6i.xlarge, while the inference job needs the larger VRAM of the A10G GPU, not just more vCPUs. Exam hook: explain why g4dn.xlarge fails the 18 GB model despite having free vCPU capacity.

slides.title: Three Launch Inputs
slides.lead: Launching a compute instance needs more than picking a size: it needs a starting operating system, a way to run setup automatically, and a way to log in securely

points.text: Machine image: OS and software template the instance boots from
User data: script that bootstraps the instance on first boot
Key pair: public/private credential for secure access
All three are chosen together when the instance is launched

slides.notes: Frame this as the three decisions made at launch time, beyond just size. Ask: which of these three decides what software is already installed? Point out each will get its own slide.

slides.title: AMI Template
slides.lead:
A machine image is a saved template of an operating system plus installed software and configuration
On AWS it is called an AMI (Amazon Machine Image), and launching from it gives every instance an identical starting state
slides.notes: Emphasise 'identical starting state' as the exam-testable idea, not just 'it has an OS'. Mention that a custom AMI is how a configured server becomes repeatable. Interview angle: why would a team build its own AMI instead of using the provider's base image?

slides.title: AMI Template
slides.notes: Emphasise 'identical starting state' as the exam-testable idea, not just 'it has an OS'. Mention that a custom AMI is how a configured server becomes repeatable. Interview angle: why would a team build its own AMI instead of using the provider's base image?

slides.title: AMI Template

points.text: Provider images: pre-built, maintained OS templates (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu)
Custom images: captured from a configured running instance
Marketplace images: vendor-packaged software bundled with an OS
Images are tied to one region and must be copied to launch elsewhere

slides.notes: Emphasise 'identical starting state' as the exam-testable idea, not just 'it has an OS'. Mention that a custom AMI is how a configured server becomes repeatable. Interview angle: why would a team build its own AMI instead of using the provider's base image?

slides.label: Analogy: a recipe card
slides.title: AMI Template
slides.notes: TR analogy: A machine image is like a recipe card with every ingredient pre-measured — just as every instance launched from it starts in the exact same state, with nothing improvised.

slides.title: First-Boot Automation
slides.lead: User data is a script supplied at launch time that the instance runs automatically once it boots, replacing manual setup after the instance appears

points.text: Passed as plain text or shell commands at launch time
Executed once by the boot-time init process, on first boot only, by default
Typical use: install packages, pull application code, start a service

slides.notes: Stress 'once, at first boot' — a common exam trap is assuming it reruns on every restart. Give the example of a script that installs a web server before anyone connects. Ask: how does a team re-run setup if the instance reboots?

slides.title: Public Private Keys
slides.lead: Cloud instances replace password login with a key pair, two mathematically linked keys that let an owner prove identity without ever sending a password over the network

points.text: Public key: installed into the instance’s authorized list at launch
Private key: downloaded once by the owner, never stored by the provider again
Password-based login is disabled by default on cloud OS images
A lost private key means lost access unless a new key is attached

slides.notes: Clarify this is asymmetric cryptography applied to login, not encryption of data. Point out the private key download is one-time only. Interview hook: why can't the provider recover a lost private key?

slides.label: Analogy: a lock and its key
slides.title: Public Private Keys
slides.notes: Analogy: A key pair is like a lock and its key — the lock (public key) stays on the instance, and only the person holding the matching key (private key) can open it.

slides.title: Image Data Key
slides.lead: Launching an instance chains the three building blocks into one sequence: the image decides what boots, the key pair decides who can log in, and user data decides what runs next

cells: Who can log in, and how
What gets configured on first boot

slides.notes: Walk the table row by row as the actual launch order. Note the AWS console surfaces all three on the same launch screen. Mention this sequence is identical whether the instance is launched manually or by an auto scaling group.

slides.title: Image Data Key
slides.notes: Walk the table row by row as the actual launch order. Note the AWS console surfaces all three on the same launch screen. Mention this sequence is identical whether the instance is launched manually or by an auto scaling group.

slides.title: ASG And Templates
slides.lead: An auto scaling group (ASG) keeps a fleet of instances at the right size automatically, using a launch template as the blueprint for every new instance it starts
slides.notes: Frame the ASG as the fleet manager and the launch template as its recipe card. Point out that every part named here gets its own detail on the next slides. Exam hook: ASG without a launch template cannot launch anything.

slides.title: ASG And Templates

points.text: Scaling policies: rules deciding when to add or remove instances
Health checks: detect and replace unhealthy instances automatically
Capacity limits: minimum, maximum and desired instance counts
Spans multiple availability zones for resilience

slides.notes: Frame the ASG as the fleet manager and the launch template as its recipe card. Point out that every part named here gets its own detail on the next slides. Exam hook: ASG without a launch template cannot launch anything.

slides.title: Versioned Blueprint
slides.lead:
Launching instances by hand means repeating the same setup each time
A launch template stores that configuration (Amazon Machine Image (AMI), instance type, key pair and security group) as a reusable, versioned blueprint the auto scaling group reads whenever it starts a new instance
slides.notes: Stress that editing a template never changes running instances — it only affects future launches. Ask: how would a bad new version be rolled back without touching live traffic? Mention this is what the ASG actually reads at launch time.

slides.title: Versioned Blueprint

points.text: Each edit creates a new numbered version
Auto scaling group launches from the version it is set to use: default, latest or a fixed number
Rolling back means pointing the group at a prior version
Replaces the older, non-versioned launch configuration format

slides.notes: Stress that editing a template never changes running instances — it only affects future launches. Ask: how would a bad new version be rolled back without touching live traffic? Mention this is what the ASG actually reads at launch time.

slides.label: Analogy: a builder's standard house plan
slides.title: Versioned Blueprint
slides.notes: TR analogy: A launch template is like a builder's standard house plan: every house built from it gets the same layout and door locks — just as every instance launched gets the same AMI, instance type and security group from the template.

slides.title: How ASG Reacts
slides.lead: Capacity sits between a minimum and maximum; a scaling policy decides how many instances run at any moment inside that range, and a cooldown stops it reacting too fast

points.text: Desired capacity: the current target instance count maintained
Health check grace period: wait before marking an instance unhealthy
Cooldown period: pause between scaling actions to let changes settle
Cost: new capacity is billed only while it actually runs

slides.notes: Walk through why target tracking suits steady load while scheduled scaling suits predictable daily patterns. Point at the cooldown bullet when explaining why a group does not scale on every single data point. Exam hook: step scaling needs defined step adjustments, target tracking does not.

slides.title: How ASG Reacts

cells: Keeps a metric near a set value
Scale up every weekday at 9 AM

slides.notes: Walk through why target tracking suits steady load while scheduled scaling suits predictable daily patterns. Point at the cooldown bullet when explaining why a group does not scale on every single data point. Exam hook: step scaling needs defined step adjustments, target tracking does not.

slides.title: EC2 Launch and Flask Deployment on Beanstalk
EC2 Plus Beanstalk
slides.lead: Launch an EC2 instance, then deploy a Flask app on Elastic Beanstalk, to compare self-managed and managed provisioning live

steps.text: Sign in to the AWS console and select the Mumbai region
Launch an EC2 instance with a chosen AMI, instance type and key pair
Connect to the instance and run basic verification commands
Package a small Flask application as a ZIP archive
Create an Elastic Beanstalk application and environment from the ZIP
Deploy and verify Version 1, then update to Version 2
Clean up every resource created to avoid charges
